profile.campus: Fayetteville, Fayette County, Georgia (QTS Fayetteville mega-campus, under development)
profile.reading:
Per Data Center Dynamics' 2022 reporting (confirming QTS as the buyer behind a previously unnamed mega-project), QTS acquired 600 acres in Fayette County, roughly 20 miles south of Atlanta, for $153.8 million ($250,000/acre); the planned campus is designed for 250MW of capacity across 1.5 million sq ft of building space, with QTS expected to invest more than $1 billion developing the site. A Baxtel listing gives 1435 Hwy 54 W, Fayetteville, GA as the campus address. The land was previously farmland that had also drawn interest from Oceanic Data Centers (approved 2020) and Facebook (which considered the site in 2018 before choosing Newton County, Georgia instead).

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and was taken private in a roughly $10 billion Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT)-led acquisition completed August 31, 2021, per Blackstone's own press release; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer. QTS's own site lists an operations support center in Suwanee, Georgia, making this Atlanta-metro cluster (Atlanta proper, Suwanee/Gwinnett County, and Fayetteville/Fayette County) an operationally significant hub for the company beyond its Northern Virginia headquarters.

Georgia Power, the state's dominant investor-owned electric utility, has flagged data center load growth in its own integrated resource plan filings with state regulators as a major driver of future generation and transmission investment, a pattern also seen among Northern Virginia's Dominion Energy and Texas's ERCOT grid operator elsewhere in this registry. Metro Atlanta's data center growth has also drawn legislative attention over sales-tax exemptions for data center equipment, a policy debate covered in Georgia trade and political press as the industry has expanded across Fulton, Gwinnett, Fayette, and neighboring counties.

reading.body:
QTS operates a unified 600-acre campus in Fayetteville spanning planned 13 to 16 buildings with a published target of 250 MW across the full development, though operating capacity of this specific facility is not confirmed. Trade press corroborates the 250 MW mega-project figure at this site. If the campus reaches the planned 250 MW of IT load, and assuming 40 kW per rack as a common AI training density, this translates to roughly 6,250 racks of accelerator capacity at full build-out, though this figure depends entirely on the customer mix and workload types QTS ultimately hosts.

Georgia has 33 mapped data center facilities with only 4 publishing power specifications, totaling 66.3 MW of disclosed capacity. This QTS campus, ranked fifth by published megawatts among Georgia facilities, would represent 377 percent of the state's currently disclosed data center IT load if it reaches 250 MW, making it the state's dominant published infrastructure asset for compute. No current operating megawatt figure from QTS's own specification pages is available to confirm what portion of the 250 MW target is live today.

The campus is not published with power supply certifications, renewable energy commitments, grid operator details, or current occupancy. QTS was acquired by Blackstone in 2021 and operates multiple sites across the Atlanta metro region. The Fayetteville location represents the operator's largest disclosed single-campus expansion plan in Georgia and sits on land with room for up to 16 buildings, though the pace and tenant composition of development beyond current operations remains unpublished.
